summary: RW Aurigae is a known young star about 509 light-years away, listed in Gaia DR3. Clouds of dust around it can block its light, so it dims unpredictably. WANDERERS found no measurable motion between 2010 and 2026; the apparent drift of 0.04 arcseconds per year is below the detection limit. SPHEREx saw no brightness change from September 2025 to March 2026 (+0.00 ± 0.07 mag). Our confidence is medium. The star is too bright for SPHEREx, so 141 of 150 measurements are flagged, and two visits can miss a dimming.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Gaia DR3 lists this star, about 509 light-years away, and catalogues already know it as a variable. From Sep 2025 to Mar 2026, its brightness changed by +0.00 ± 0.07 mag. That is smaller than the uncertainty, so it looked quiet. Its 0.1-pixel shift is too small to measure. Confidence is only medium because 141 of 150 measurements are flagged as too bright. Two snapshots can also miss dimming that happens between them.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: Three things lower my confidence. 141 of 150 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because the star is too bright, so brightness comes from the faint edges of its image, uncertain by about 0.07 magnitudes. SPHEREx visited only twice, in Sep 2025 and Mar 2026, so a dimming between visits could go unseen. The measured drift disagrees with Gaia's, but it is only a tenth of a pixel, too small to trust.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE imaged this sky around 2010, and SPHEREx imaged it in 2025 and 2026. The 16-year gap lets even slow stars drift far enough to measure. RW Aurigae shifted only 0.62 arcseconds, about a tenth of a SPHEREx pixel. That is too small to count as real motion. SPHEREx also splits light into many colors, but this star is too bright: 141 of 150 measurements are flagged.
